name: Marx's theory of alienation
summary: Marx's theory holds that in a society built on private property and wage labour, people are separated from the product of their work, from the activity of working, from other people and from their own creative human nature, and that this separation is a social ill to be ended by transforming material life, not by correcting ideas. Productive activity under communism is predicted to be unalienated. Later Marxian writers extended it to consumption, culture and politics.
scope: The theory of alienation (estranged labour) that Marx first set out in the 1844 Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts and its later development in the Marxian tradition: the four dimensions of alienated labour under capitalism (from the product, the activity, other people, and species-being), religion and the state as expressions of it, fetishism as one of its forms, and its overcoming in communist society (SEP 'Alienation' and 'Karl Marx', Britannica, Mészáros's book-length study). It is the Marxian line defined by those sources, including Western Marxist extensions (Lukács, Marcuse). It excludes Marxism as a whole, other theories of alienation (the sociological 'mass society' stream, Seeman's subjective measures, Hegel's and Feuerbach's own versions, Western alienation as a regional grievance), and the Althusserian view that the humanist concept was abandoned.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: In 'Needs, Production and Division of Labour' (Manuscripts) Marx calls the division of labour the economic expression of the social character of labour within estrangement. Mészáros (Part II, economic aspects, around p.143) reports that Marx treats it as applying only to alienated conditions, and that once life-activity is no longer regulated by private property and exchange the social character of labour shows itself without the alienating mediation of the division of labour. The sources do not spell out a regime with no specialised jobs at all, so the answer is moderate.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: In 'Estranged Labour' Marx writes that wages are a direct consequence of estranged labour and that estranged labour is the direct cause of private property, so the downfall of one must involve the downfall of the other; an enforced raise in wages would be 'nothing but better payment for the slave'. 'Private Property and Communism' (Manuscripts) holds that alienation is overcome only by the positive transcendence of private property. Mészáros, Part II on the economic aspects, reads the theory the same way.

notes: Themes searched in the 1844 Manuscripts (Progress Publishers and the marxists.org 'Estranged Labour' text), Mészáros, SEP 'Alienation' and 'Karl Marx', Britannica: economy (property, wages, division of labour, money, needs), religion, state, history, means. Money, class struggle, historical materialism, the state as class instrument and revolution belong to Marx's wider thought or to Marxism and are left null here; Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man was found but not cited as it extends the theory and is a key work only through SEP. Althusser's For Marx is a critic's reading and was not used.
